assessment.nobel_worthiness: Foundational and wide-reaching. Their political-economy model of trade policy ('Protection for Sale') and their joint work on innovation, growth and trade reshaped both theory and applied work on trade agreements and lobbying. The theory is rigorous and has also shaped empirical work and policy debate. It resembles the kind of practically useful theory that has been honored before.
assessment.attribution: The two are a clear, natural pair with decades of joint work. Helpman's separate firm-heterogeneity work appears elsewhere on the list, but the core protection and growth contributions are jointly authored and cleanly credited to these two.
assessment.maturity: Very mature. The key papers date from the late 1980s to the 1990s and have been tested, extended and taught for three decades. There is no timing concern.
uncertainties: Krugman's 2008 prize and Melitz-type firm-heterogeneity work may make the committee reluctant to honor trade again soon.
Part of the impact is conceptual rather than directly policy-changing.
Helpman's role in the firm-heterogeneity literature could prompt a different laureate grouping.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki–Moore (1997) gave the canonical account of how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. It became the workhorse of macro-finance and informed policy thinking after 2008. The link to incomplete contracts and financial contracting is strong, and the theory has since been tested on real credit-market data.
assessment.attribution: The central credit-cycles model is jointly authored by Kiyotaki and Moore. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the related financial-accelerator tradition, but Bernanke's 2022 prize already recognized much of that line. Limiting the proposal to the two originators gives the cleanest attribution.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Nearly three decades of citations and extensions, with strong post-crisis empirical validation of the mechanisms.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize for banks and financial crises (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig) could weigh against recognition.
The committee might prefer to include Gertler, which would dilute the attribution.
Empirical identification of collateral channels is still debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The BLP demand-estimation framework, with Pakes's dynamic industry models, transformed empirical industrial organization. It is now the standard tool in merger review, antitrust and regulation, and in applied work across fields. The impact on both methods and practice is substantial.
assessment.attribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes are the authors of the BLP papers, and Pakes also led the dynamic-games and estimation work. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin made real contributions, but the three-name set captures the core of the method most cleanly.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The methods date from the 1990s and are now routine in competition policy and in teaching.
uncertainties: The three-laureate limit forces the exclusion of Bresnahan and others, so credit is contestable.
Some of the impact is methodological and concentrated in one subfield.
The committee has not recently honored industrial organization, which could cut either way.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The law-and-finance program created a vast literature linking legal origins and investor protection to financial development, ownership structure and growth. It shaped corporate governance research and policy, and I know the empirical corporate-finance side of it well. Its influence is very high even though the conclusions are debated.
assessment.attribution: The core papers are by La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny. A three-person limit forces a choice, and Vishny's contribution is also substantial. The approach is empirical and cross-country, so credit is spread across many co-authors.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The work dates from 1997–2008 and has had a long period of replication, critique and refinement.
uncertainties: Robustness and measurement of the legal-origins indices have been seriously challenged, and the causal interpretation remains contested.
Shleifer's Harvard–Russia episode may weigh on the committee.
Excluding Vishny is a debatable choice.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: They built long-run series on top incomes and wealth from tax data and reshaped the empirical and public debate on inequality. This was a major data and measurement advance, and it helped open a new research agenda. The theory behind the policy conclusions is less settled than the measurement.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the pioneers of the top-income series, and Zucman extended the work to wealth and offshore holdings. Atkinson, who is now deceased, was an important precursor, and the work builds on a wider set of collaborators. Saez also appears under the taxation candidate, so credit is shared.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature for the income series (since 2003) and less mature for the wealth and offshore estimates (2010s–2020s). Methodological critiques are still being resolved.
uncertainties: Measurement debates over the wealth-share estimates and the treatment of taxes and transfers remain open.
The policy conclusions are politically charged, and the analytical contribution beyond data construction is arguable.
Zucman's work is relatively recent.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Large-scale administrative data on mobility and neighborhood effects have changed the empirical study of opportunity, taxation and place. The research is highly influential on policy, and the data-driven approach has been widely adopted. The work has had very high impact across several fields.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear leader, with Hendren and Friedman as the closest collaborators on the mobility and neighborhood-effects papers. Katz's earlier Moving to Opportunity work is an important input but is distinct. Credit is spread across a large team.
assessment.maturity: Moderate. Most of the key results are from 2014 onward. Replication and the long-term effects of place-based findings are still developing.
uncertainties: The work may be too recent and may overlap with the Card and Angrist–Imbens credibility revolution already recognized.
Questions remain about the causal interpretation of neighborhood-effect estimates.
Heavy reliance on proprietary administrative data limits independent replication.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Formal models of present bias and reference dependence extended the behavioral program beyond Kahneman (2002) and Thaler (2017). They are applied to savings, pension design, contracts and consumer finance, which fits the practical impact that prior behavioral prizes stressed. The conceptual and applied reach is broad.
assessment.attribution: Laibson and Rabin are central to the quasi-hyperbolic and psychology-based modeling lines. Koszegi, with Rabin, developed the reference-dependent preference model. O'Donoghue and Loewenstein have strong claims, so the three-person limit creates a hard attribution problem.
assessment.maturity: Mature in concept, with core papers from the 1990s and 2000s and extensive applications. Field evidence for some mechanisms, such as present bias in naive agents, is still mixed.
uncertainties: Behavioral economics has been honored twice, which may reduce appetite.
The credit division among Laibson, Rabin, O'Donoghue, Loewenstein and Koszegi is unclear.
Replication and structural-estimation debates about present bias and loss aversion persist.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model (Rubinstein 1982) and the market-bargaining models built on it are foundational. They underlie work on contracting, labor markets, search and decentralized trade, and the theory is clean and widely used. Rubinstein's broader contributions in game theory and bounded rationality add weight.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein is the clear originator. Wolinsky is credited through the Rubinstein–Wolinsky market-bargaining model. Binmore made important related contributions, but the central result is Rubinstein's.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature. Four decades of use and extension, with the model standard in textbooks.
uncertainties: Nash, Harsanyi and Selten (1994) and later game theory prizes may have already covered some of this ground.
It is unclear whether the committee would see pure theory of this type as having enough empirical or policy impact now.
Whether to include Wolinsky or Binmore alongside Rubinstein is debatable.
